units.title: Replica serving and tensor-parallel inference shapes and collectives
outcomes: Distinguish independent serving replicas from ranks cooperating on one forward pass, including their request-level fault domains.
Derive local MLP and attention projection shapes for a tensor-parallel serving plan.
Place forward collectives and explain why added memory capacity need not reduce small-batch latency.
units.why: A router distributes requests across replicas; tensor parallelism distributes one request's model work across ranks. Confusing the two gives the wrong capacity estimate and the wrong recovery boundary.

next.note: Turn the shard shapes into per-rank ownership and memory budgets.

study.title: Replicas versus model shards
study.locator: Chapter 7, Data Parallelism, printed pp. 243 to 245; Tensor Parallelism and Pipeline Parallelism, printed pp. 245 to 250
study.depth: Read the replica and TP paths now. Leave the pipeline decision path for the next unit; do not run the multi-GPU launch snippet.

study.title: The paired column and row shards
study.locator: Module 09, Tensor parallelism: split inside the layer - The MLP block and The attention block
study.depth: Stop before Communication volume. Two reductions per layer describes this replicated-activation dense forward schedule, not every TP implementation.

focus: Reuse Collective contracts and the latency-bandwidth cost model. Serving replicas do not synchronize gradients; a replica can itself contain a TP group.

For input \(X\) of shape \(T 	imes h\), column-shard the first MLP weight of shape \(h 	imes f\), then row-shard the second of shape \(f 	imes h\). Each local intermediate has shape \(T 	imes f/n\) for divisible width and \(n\) ranks.
An elementwise activation stays local between these shards. The second projection produces same-shaped partial outputs that sum, not concatenate. Add a replicated output bias once after summation.
Attention head shards can compute independently before the output projection reduction. KV-head replication and vocabulary-parallel output paths need separate ownership accounting.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive a bias-free two-rank ReLU MLP with input shape \(2 	imes 4\), first weight shape \(4 	imes 6\) and second weight shape \(6 	imes 4\). Give each rank three intermediate features, sum its partial output, and check against the unsharded MLP on CPU using small deterministic float64 tensors. State a numerical tolerance rather than demanding bitwise equality.
traps: Counting replicas as additional memory for a single request. Each independent replica needs the full model and its own admitted KV state.
Calling every column-sharded output an all-reduce. Disjoint output features concatenate; row-sharded dot-product contributions sum.
Promising a latency speedup from rank count. Smaller kernels, startup costs and dependencies can consume the extra compute or memory bandwidth.

selfTest.q: Does inference replica serving require the training gradient all-reduce?
selfTest.a: No. Independent requests run forward passes against fixed weights. Shared routing or cache metadata is a separate control-plane concern.

selfTest.q: Why can the first projection's activation remain local?
selfTest.a: Each rank owns complete values for its output features, and ReLU acts independently on each feature. No partial sum is needed before that activation.

selfTest.q: What shape does each second-projection partial have in the reproduce example?
selfTest.a: \(2 	imes 4\). Each rank multiplies a \(2 	imes 3\) intermediate by its \(3 	imes 4\) weight rows; the two partials sum to the full output.

selfTest.q: Can replicas lower endpoint latency without making the forward pass faster?
selfTest.a: Yes. Distributing arrivals can reduce queueing. It does not shorten the isolated forward service time on an unchanged replica.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: servelab's replica and TP plans, local-shape ledger and differential checks against an unsharded forward pass.
units.stopWhen: Your paired-shard MLP matches the unsharded reference within the stated tolerance, and your diagram separates replica routing from TP collectives and their fault domains.

fit.note: The book's replica and sharding sections and Module 09's paired MLP cover the serving distinction and forward shapes; servelab supplies CPU differential practice.

units.title: Pipeline bubbles, expert-parallel MoE and context parallelism in serving
outcomes: Derive a forward-only pipeline timeline and identify the concurrency and stage balance needed to fill it.
Map MoE dispatch and combine to serving ranks, preserving the selected experts and routing weights.
Distinguish layer, expert, head and context-position partitioning, including the communication exact attention still needs.
units.why: PP, EP and context parallelism partition different axes. Their serving value depends on available concurrency, expert skew and context length, not just whether the model fits.

next.note: Price each dependency on the topology that carries it.

study.title: Pipeline and expert serving paths
study.locator: Chapter 15, Pipeline Parallelism; Expert Parallelism; Dynamic Routing Strategies for MoE Inference - Expert Communication Optimization and Load Balancing, Capacity Factor, and Expert Replication
study.depth: Focus on serving dependencies and placement. Do not change the model's chosen experts to fix load: rerouting or dropping expert work changes outputs.

study.title: Partitioning cached positions
study.locator: Module 09, Decode context parallelism: shard the cache by position, not by head - The mechanism, one decode step and Why decode specifically
study.depth: Stop before the version-specific vLLM constraints and reported benchmark. Use the online-softmax merge from Stable and online softmax, normalization and fused residual paths, not a plain sum of locally normalized attention.

study.title: A forward pipeline bubble exercise
study.locator: Day 17, Pipeline Parallelism: layer blocks + the bubble; Try These Experiments, item 4, PP bubble break-even
study.depth: Only this timeline and exercise. Assume equal forward stage times and independent microbatches; do not import a training backward schedule.

focus: Reuse All-to-all and MoE dispatch, combine and load balance. In serving, small decode batches can expose startup and hot-expert delay even when the aggregate dispatch byte count is small.

With \(p\) equal stages, \(m\) ready independent microbatches and stage time \(t\), a transfer-free forward pipeline finishes in \((m+p-1)t\). Idle fraction is \((p-1)/(m+p-1)\); autoregressive feedback and uneven stage times invalidate that simple schedule.

Expert placement changes which assignments cross a slow link. Replicating the same expert preserves its function; changing top-k choices or overflow semantics does not automatically preserve model quality.

Context parallelism partitions positions; TP commonly partitions heads. Exact global attention still incorporates every permitted position using communicated KV blocks or partial softmax statistics. Sequence parallelism can instead mean partitioning intermediate activations around TP - state the axis, not just the acronym.
units.reproduce: Draw the transfer-free forward timeline for four equal 2 ms stages and eight ready independent microbatches. Recover a 22 ms makespan and idle fraction \(3/11\). Then add the dependency from the final sampled token to the same request's next decode pass and explain why eight successive tokens of one request cannot fill the pipeline like eight independent microbatches.
traps: Using a full-training pipeline bubble formula for forward-only inference, or treating future tokens of one request as already available microbatches.
Placing paired hot experts together without checking compute imbalance. Fewer remote bytes can still leave one rank on the critical path.
Summing locally normalized attention outputs. Each slice has a different softmax normalizer; exact merging must reweight them.

selfTest.q: Does PP make four equal stages execute one isolated request simultaneously?
selfTest.a: No. Its activations traverse all four stages in order. Other independent requests can occupy the remaining stages; the isolated request retains the full dependency chain.

selfTest.q: Why is an expert replica different from rerouting to another expert?
selfTest.a: A replica computes the same expert function with the same weights. A different expert generally computes a different function, changing the model output.

selfTest.q: Do position shards let exact causal attention ignore distant earlier positions?
selfTest.a: No. Those positions remain legal keys. Their contributions must reach the query through KV exchange or a correctly normalized partial-result merge.

selfTest.q: What does a slow PP stage do to steady-state capacity?
selfTest.a: It limits the rate at which microbatches can leave the pipeline. More stages or a low average stage time cannot remove that bottleneck.

practice.name: 100 Days of Inference, Day 17: PP bubble break-even
practice.locator: Try These Experiments, item 4: find the minimum microbatch count for idle fraction strictly below 10 percent with 4, 8 and 16 stages
practice.note: Check your integer boundary by enumerating the forward timeline on CPU. The notebook has no public grader; add your own tests. The section mini-project covers expert skew and context-partition accounting.

units.stopWhen: Your timeline agrees with the hand makespan and each integer bubble boundary, and you can name the partition axis, communication dependency and serving bottleneck for PP, EP and context parallelism.

fit.note: The book covers PP, EP and topology-aware expert placement, Module 09 supplies exact position-shard merging, and the named Day 17 exercise gives CPU timeline practice.

units.title: Weight and KV sharding and per-rank memory ownership
outcomes: Derive each rank's weight and KV bytes from the actual layer, head and position ownership rather than dividing everything by device count.
Explain KV-head replication when TP exceeds the number of KV heads in a head-sharded GQA layout.
Reject a plan whose busiest rank exceeds memory after runtime buffers, page waste and reserve are included.
units.why: Aggregate memory is not admission capacity. One rank can run out of KV space while other ranks have free memory, and replicated state can erase an expected sharding gain.

next.note: Use the ownership ledger to count source and destination transfer fragments.

study.title: Head sharding and the GQA ceiling
study.locator: Module 09, What TP degree actually does to your numbers - Weights per GPU and KV cache per GPU stops shrinking at TP-8
study.depth: Use the head-ownership argument only. Skip the hardware speed table and Code lab planner: evenly divided weights are an approximation, and its PP latency estimate does not sum the dependent stage service times.

study.title: Layer and expert ownership
study.locator: Chapter 15, Tensor Parallelism, Pipeline Parallelism, Expert Parallelism and Data Parallelism
study.depth: Revisit only which weights each rank holds. Carry forward the runtime-memory categories from Weight memory by dtype and the runtime memory categories.

focus: Reuse Per-layer KV layouts and the cache consequences of attention variants. For ordinary full-attention K and V, a rank owning \(L_r\) layers, \(H_r\) KV heads and \(S_r\) cached positions holds \(2L_rH_rd_hbS_r\) logical bytes, where \(d_h\) is head dimension and \(b\) is bytes per element.

PP assigns KV to the ranks that own its layers. Head-sharded TP assigns local KV heads; if there are more TP ranks than KV heads, a supported layout may replicate heads instead of shrinking each cache further.
EP partitions expert weights, not automatically attention weights or KV. Sum shared, expert, embedding and output weights according to the chosen layout; include replicated tensors explicitly.
Admission uses the maximum per-rank allocation, including page rounding, workspace, graphs, communication buffers and reserve. Distinguish logical unique KV from physical copies across ranks.
units.reproduce: Make a per-rank ledger for a synthetic full-attention model with eight layers, two KV heads, head dimension 16, two-byte KV elements and one 128-token sequence. Its unique KV is 131,072 bytes. Under two-way head-sharded TP each rank holds 65,536 bytes; under four-way TP with each KV head replicated twice, each rank still holds 65,536 bytes. Add two-way PP with four layers per stage and recompute local and aggregate physical bytes. Ignore page waste only for this logical-byte exercise.
traps: Dividing all memory by the product of TP, PP and EP sizes. Only the tensors actually partitioned along those axes get that divisor.
Treating a head-count ceiling as a universal limit on usable devices. Position sharding can reduce cache further, but requires its own layout and communication contract.
Checking total free memory instead of each rank's budget. The first exhausted rank can stop the whole serving group.

selfTest.q: In the four-way TP example, how many physical KV bytes exist across ranks?
selfTest.a: 262,144 bytes, twice the unique KV. Each of the two KV heads has two physical copies.

selfTest.q: Does expert parallelism alone divide dense attention KV by expert count?
selfTest.a: No. Experts belong to the MoE feed-forward path. Attention KV follows attention layer, head and position ownership.

selfTest.q: How does two-way PP change each TP rank's KV in this equal-layer example?
selfTest.a: It halves local KV to 32,768 bytes because each stage owns four of the eight layers. Aggregate physical KV stays unchanged for the same TP replication pattern.

selfTest.q: Why is weight bytes divided by rank count insufficient to prove a plan fits?
selfTest.a: Some weights are replicated or unevenly placed, and KV, temporary tensors, communication buffers and runtime reserve also consume local memory.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: servelab's rank ownership ledger, replicated-head cases and memory-feasibility tests before admitting requests.
units.stopWhen: Your ledger reconciles unique and physical KV bytes for TP, PP and their combination, and rejects a plan that fails any local memory budget.

fit.note: The pool's head-sharding explanation and book ownership sections support the local-byte derivation; servelab checks replicated and uneven layouts without extra devices.

units.title: Communication volume, topology, and small-batch latency against capacity
outcomes: Derive per-decode-step and per-prefill-pass collective and stage-boundary traffic with an explicit per-rank or aggregate convention.
Map that traffic onto PCIe, NVLink, NVSwitch and network paths, including shared bottleneck links.
Explain when more ranks provide memory capacity but increase small-batch latency after communication startup and dependencies are included.
units.why: Serving decode repeatedly pays small collective startup costs. A topology that fits the model can still miss the token-latency target even when its bandwidth-only estimate looks cheap.

next.note: Use the exposed communication model to constrain phase placement.

study.title: Serving activation traffic
study.locator: Module 09, Tensor parallelism: split inside the layer - Communication volume; Pipeline parallelism: split across layers - Communication is tiny; Math by hand, Parts 3 and 4
study.depth: Do the byte arithmetic, not the supplied hardware time estimates. The page mixes directional and bidirectional link peaks and calls a whole decode batch step's traffic per-token traffic. Use per-step bytes, a declared directional effective bandwidth and the startup term from your GPU communication model.

study.title: Placement across links and nodes
study.locator: Chapter 7, Tensor Parallelism and Pipeline Parallelism, printed pp. 247 to 250, Figures 7-10 and 7-11
study.depth: Treat the flowchart as candidate generation, not proof that TP needs NVLink or that a single-device plan always wins. Check the declared SLO and actual topology.

focus: Reuse Ring and tree all-reduce, all-gather and reduce-scatter volume, Interconnects and topology: PCIe, NVLink, NVSwitch and RDMA, and NCCL algorithms, protocols, channels and rank placement. New work here is multiplying those costs by serving-layer frequency.

For a replicated-activation dense schedule, message size is \(M = BShb\), with batch size \(B\), processed positions per sequence \(S\), hidden width \(h\) and bytes per element \(b\). Decode has \(S = 1\); prefill uses its scheduled prompt or chunk length.

With \(n\) ranks, ring all-reduce sends \(2(n-1)M/n\) bytes per rank. Two reductions per layer over \(L\) layers cost \(2L\) matched collectives per pass. This is an implementation assumption, not a universal transformer law.

Use \(2(n-1)\alpha + 2(n-1)M/(nW)\) for a simple ring model with per-step startup \(\alpha\) and directional effective bandwidth \(W\). PP sends one activation per stage boundary and retains the serial stage path. Shared links, uneven ranks and overlap change exposed time.
units.reproduce: For a synthetic eight-layer dense forward pass with batch size 2, hidden width 64, two-byte activations and four TP ranks, derive the decode message size of 256 bytes and ring egress of 384 bytes per rank per reduction. Two reductions per layer give 6,144 bytes per rank per batch step. Recompute for a 128-position prefill, then compare both startup and bandwidth terms using declared synthetic link parameters. Count PP traffic separately per boundary, not as a ring reduction.
traps: Calling batch-step wire bytes bytes per output token without dividing by the number of active sequences. A step can generate many tokens, while each request still waits for the complete step.
Using bidirectional aggregate peak as one rank's send bandwidth, or adding send and receive bytes and comparing them to a one-direction rate.
Assuming a node count identifies the fabric. TP groups inside one node may cross slow PCIe or socket paths, while some NVLink domains span multiple nodes.

selfTest.q: What changes when the example processes 128 positions instead of one?
selfTest.a: The activation message and bandwidth term grow 128-fold. The assumed collective count and each collective's startup term do not. Kernel efficiency and attention cost can also change.

selfTest.q: Why can a tiny decode message still make TP slow?
selfTest.a: Many dependent collectives repeatedly pay startup and wait for the slowest participating rank. Dividing only bytes by bandwidth omits those costs.

selfTest.q: Does PP's smaller traffic prove it has lower isolated-request latency?
selfTest.a: No. The request still traverses every stage sequentially and pays stage-boundary transfers. Its benefit may instead be model capacity or throughput with enough independent work.

selfTest.q: What must change in the model when two transfers share one NIC?
selfTest.a: Their combined offered bytes compete for that NIC's directional capacity. They cannot both receive its full effective bandwidth at the same time.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: servelab's per-layer communication ledger, shared-link model and small-batch latency versus memory-capacity sweep.
units.stopWhen: Your byte ledger reconciles per-rank and aggregate traffic, and your synthetic sweep identifies a capacity-feasible TP plan that loses latency after startup is restored.

fit.note: The pool's explicit serving traffic arithmetic and placement flowchart cover the derivation when units and directionality are corrected; servelab supplies topology sweeps.

units.title: Replica routing, load balance and cache-locality skew
outcomes: Implement a deterministic cache-aware router that checks capacity before applying locality and load tie-breaks.
Compare load-only and cache-aware decisions under hot-prefix skew, changing reuse and stale worker information.
Diagnose a higher cache-hit rate that worsens queueing, fairness or SLO-qualified completions.
units.why: A warm prefix saves prefill work but can attract enough requests to overload its owner. Routing must value the saved work against waiting and capacity, not maximize hits alone.

next.note: Split routing and admission across prefill and decode pools.

study.locator: Chapter 7, Data Parallelism, printed pp. 244 to 245 - round robin, least connections, latency-based and cache-aware routing

study.title: Balance predicted waiting against cache reuse
study.locator: FAST 25 paper, Section 4.1 Prefill Global Scheduling and Section 4.2 Cache Load Balancing, printed pp. 161 to 162
study.depth: Study the decision rule and hot-cache replication. Leave the cluster experiments and their numerical results out of your local routing claims.

study.title: Worker selection at phase boundaries
study.locator: Dynamo v1.5.1, Efficient KV Transfer - Router Orchestration, steps 1 to 4

focus: Build on Exact prefix identity, version scope and tenant privacy scope. A cache overlap score is useful only for compatible, authorized KV; it is not permission to reuse another tenant's state.
Track full assigned token capacity separately from uncached prefill work. Reuse saves computation but does not make the destination request's complete context disappear.

The TensorTonic problem prioritizes the longest cached prefix before projected uncached load. Mooncake instead minimizes predicted TTFT including waiting; these are different policies, not equivalent implementations.
Worker discovery, cache events and load estimates can lag. Revalidate capacity and identity at admission, and keep a fallback for evicted prefixes or unavailable workers.
units.reproduce: Implement the named TensorTonic rule from a blank file. Check feasibility using full assigned request lengths, then rank by longest prefix, lowest projected uncached load, most remaining capacity and smallest worker ID. Reproduce the public example with request lengths `[10, 8]`, prefix lengths `[[8, 0], [0, 6]]`, worker IDs `[2, 1]` and capacities `[20, 20]`: assignments `[2, 1]` and uncached loads `[2, 2]`. Then construct a queued hot-prefix case where a predicted-TTFT policy deliberately chooses less reuse.
traps: Using uncached tokens as the memory-admission cost. The public rule admits against the full assigned request length even when most tokens have a prefix hit.
Interpreting a router's hit estimate as guaranteed resident KV. Eviction or worker restart between selection and admission can invalidate it.
Improving aggregate TTFT while starving tenants with cold prefixes. Compare waiting and completions by tenant or request class.

selfTest.q: A six-token request has a four-token cache hit on a worker with capacity five. Is it feasible under the problem's rule?
selfTest.a: No. Full assigned length, six tokens, exceeds capacity five. The two uncached tokens determine compute load, not feasibility.

selfTest.q: Why can longest-prefix routing lose to load-only routing?
selfTest.a: A hot cache owner can have enough waiting work to outweigh the saved prefill. Low reuse or stale cache information can also remove the expected saving.

selfTest.q: Two workers tie on prefix, projected work and remaining capacity. What breaks the public problem's tie?
selfTest.a: The smaller worker ID, not the first worker in the input array. Returned loads remain in input-worker order.

selfTest.q: Does replicating a hot prefix always improve goodput?
selfTest.a: No. It costs memory and transfer work, can evict useful other prefixes and may not relieve the current compute or queue bottleneck. Test it on the same arrival trace.

practice.name: TensorTonic: Route Cache-Aware Prefill Requests
practice.note: The free public cases check cache-local choices, worker-ID tie-breaking and rejection when no worker fits. Add tests for projected-load and remaining-capacity ties yourself. The section mini-project compares this locality-first rule with load-only and predicted-TTFT routing.

units.stopWhen: Your router passes the three public cases and your additional tie-break tests, and your hot-prefix counterexample explains why saved prefill does not guarantee lower waiting or better goodput.

fit.note: The book and Mooncake cover locality versus load, Dynamo supplies current phase routing, and the verified free TensorTonic problem anchors deterministic implementation practice.
